An April 1966 special report in the CIA's Current Intelligence Weekly takes up the problems of the Czechoslovak Communist Party. The title trails off mid-phrase in the file, but the subject is clear enough: the party that ran Czechoslovakia was in trouble. The report appeared two years before the Prague Spring.

The party's problems, as the agency framed them, grew out of reform pressure inside a system built on tight control. Analysts were watching for cracks in the Soviet bloc, and Czechoslovakia was showing them early. The report matters because it shows the strain was visible long before the famous reform movement of 1968 made headlines around the world.
cia-0000126978: A June 1975 CIA National Intelligence Bulletin covers Angola. The bulletin was the agency's daily product for top officials, and this issue took up a colony five months from independence. Rival armies were already racing for the capital, Luanda, as the issue went out. Daily bulletins reached the president's table, so an Angola issue in June placed the colony's race for power before the highest readers in the government that day.
cia-0000132178: Situation report 494, from January 1991, covers political developments including Soviets evacuating, the heading breaking off. Soviet advisers had served in Iraq for years, and their leaving marked Moscow's distance from Saddam. The report tracks that withdrawal. cia-0000126878: Dated around August 1968, this CIA document studies the short-run economic effects of the Soviet occupation of Czechoslovakia, the heading breaking off. Nuclear arms in the Middle East would pose a grave threat, warns Resolution A/69/78, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text takes note of the latest vote of the world atomic body's main meeting, in September 2014. It presses the urgent need to place all atomic plants in the region under the full checks of that body, the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The vote recalls the 1995 world meeting on the pact against the spread of nuclear arms. There, states urged all lands to join the pact at the soonest date. The call falls hardest on the states of the region that run atomic plants no world check has seen. That hint, at Israel's plant at Dimona, is plain to all who read it.
un-sc-res-1378: Entered in the record as Resolution 1378, this Security Council text is catalogued at 2001. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1478: Formal decisions of the Security Council carry numbers, and 1478 is this one's place in the sequence. The text is preserved as an English Wikisource transcription of the United Nations record. Within it, the fifteen members set out the facts they acted on, then vote the orders and requests that follow from those findings into effect.
un-sc-res-1678: Security Council Resolution 1678 is preserved in this collection in the official wording transcribed by English Wikisource. A resolution's life begins in negotiation and ends in the record; only the record version binds. The text kept here is that version, opening findings through closing instructions, with nothing summarized away or paraphrased.
un-sc-res-1778:
War in Sudan's Darfur region spilled into Chad, and Resolution 1778 sent a UN mission to guard the border camps. Hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced Chadians lived there in harsh conditions. The Council acted in 2007 to protect them.

The new mission, MINURCAT, was mostly police and support staff rather than combat troops, working beside Chadian officers and a European force. Its duties covered camp security, aid routes, and the rule of law in the east. The text shows how one country's war can pull peacekeepers into its neighbor's territory.
un-sc-res-1878: In 2009 the Council passed Resolution 1878, preserved in this collection as an official-record text via Wikisource. The genre demands economy: a few pages must carry findings, law, and instructions at once. This entry shows the economy at work and preserves it whole, so the act can be read as its addressees read it.
cia-0000132778: Washington filed a third paper on Cuba and the Caribbean on August 4, 1960, and this briefing is that entry. cia-0000135678: Dated 2 November 1960, this Spanish text is one of several 2506 Brigade documents bearing that same date in the declassified release. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d78: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on October 30, 1943, his second letter to China's leader in four days. It is Document 78 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Cairo meeting, where Chiang would sit with Roosevelt and Churchill, was now set for late November, and the letters of these weeks arranged it. The record gives the date and the names. The text in the Foreign Relations series holds the details.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d178: American delegation minutes of the final meeting of the Moscow Conference, held on October 30, 1943, form Document 178 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The final session sealed three weeks of talks and set the texts the ministers signed that day. Minutes of a closing meeting carry the formal end of a story the letters in this volume tell in pieces. The volume prints them in the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d278:
A long Cairo meeting of 26 November 1943 left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The Log dates the start at half past four, but other accounts suggest it ran at least two hours, with Churchill and the Chiangs at Roosevelt's villa for much of the afternoon.

Elliott Roosevelt describes a final political conference in the garden, with Harriman, Eden, and Cadogan present, framing the words of the Cairo communiqué. For security, that statement was held back until after Tehran, and until Stalin approved its text. Stilwell's account adds that Chiang agreed to Burma points he had rejected the day before. The note closes with a long list of other Roosevelt-Chiang topics, from a billion-dollar loan to the Chengtu airfield costs.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d378:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a private talk between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at twenty past three. Roosevelt had asked Stalin to come to him to speak briefly and frankly, and the subject was American domestic politics.

Roosevelt explains that an election falls in 1944, that he may have to run again if the war continues. Six or seven million Americans of Polish descent must not be lost as voters. Personally he favors moving Poland's eastern border west and her western border to the Oder, but he cannot join any decision at Tehran or speak publicly now. On the Baltic states, he jokes he will not go to war when Soviet armies reoccupy them, but asks for some public expression of the people's will in time. Stalin answers that chances for that will come under the Soviet constitution, with no international control.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d478:
A further memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date December 4, 1943, the first day of the Second Cairo Conference. The American chiefs were pressing to convert the broad Tehran understandings into fixed plans. The State Department included the paper in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Written positions mattered at Cairo because the two allies still differed over the balance between the cross-Channel attack and operations in the Mediterranean. The American chiefs stated their case in papers like this before arguing it in session. For readers, the memorandum is evidence from inside that argument, showing how the United States framed its demands at the summit's military level.
frus-1944-quebec-d78: The editorial note listed as Document 78 was drafted by State Department historians. It sits inside the Quebec 1944 volume of conference papers. Editorial notes explain what the documents leave unsaid. They give background and point readers to related records in the series. Behind the note stands the September 1944 Quebec meeting. Roosevelt hosted Churchill there as Allied armies entered Germany. The note guides readers through the preparations for that summit.
frus-1944-quebec-d178:
What passed between Roosevelt and Churchill at lunch on September 13, 1944, is known only at second hand. The editors draw on a memorandum by Harry White, the Treasury official, recording what Roosevelt told Morgenthau later that day. Churchill had been very glum during the conversation, according to this account.

Roosevelt said he had asked Churchill how he would like to have the steel business of Europe for twenty or thirty years. Churchill, he reported, seemed much excited over the possibility. The note also records a suggestion made at one of the day's meetings: that Fiorello La Guardia go to Italy as the president's representative and attend meetings of the Allied Control Commission.
frus-1944-quebec-d278: A one-sentence British memorandum, C.C.S. 682 of September 15, 1944, asks the American chiefs to take note of a single fact: Operation Highball would be available in the Eastern Theatre at the end of November 1944. The Combined Chiefs noted the paper at their 175th meeting the same day. No details of the operation are given in the memorandum itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d78:
Two open items had to be settled before a United Nations conference could even be called. Acting Secretary Stettinius told the President so on 15 November 1944, in a memorandum printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The items were Security Council voting and invitations with initial membership.

Stettinius then lists the ways to reach agreement. The most promising, he writes, is a meeting of the three heads of government. Failing that, the three foreign ministers might meet, preferably in London. A third option sends the Under Secretary to London. The paper is a direct step toward the Big Three meeting that became Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d178:
A way out of the Yugoslav deadlock appeared on 27 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew's top secret report to the Secretary of State, traveling with the President's party, carries the news in excerpt. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Subasic has accepted King Peter's latest proposal. The exile government will resign and be formed again at once under Subasic, on a wider basis. The new government will then put the Tito–Subasic agreement into force, taking account of the King's two objections. If the counter-proposal fails, the King will agree to the regency clause instead. Tito has consented to Subasic's coming to Belgrade to carry the agreement out, the appointment of a regency among the steps. Subasic plans to leave on 29 January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d278:
Prisoners of war head the matters Winant put to Stettinius on 28 January 1945. His letter from London, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, was written on the eve of the conference. The Russians, he explains, feel deeply about this problem, and the letter shows why.

Hundreds of thousands of Soviet people, brutally treated by the Germans, are being freed in growing numbers by the allied armies. Moscow is pressing London and Washington, through the military missions, for two-way agreements. Each government would treat the other's freed nationals by the standard it applies to its own soldiers. Civilians count the same as soldiers in the Russian view. Winant adds a confession of difficulty. The European Advisory Commission never got to grips with the question. Its special subcommittee never met, for want of instructions to him.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d378: Get this referred to the foreign ministers before there is trouble. That is the whole of Harry Hopkins's advice to the President in this note of February 7, 1945, passed during the fourth plenary meeting. The slip is one sentence long, signed with Hopkins's first name. Its link to that session rests on internal evidence and on a later account the editors cite. Small as it is, the note shows the adviser steering a heated debate toward the ministers' table, where bargains could be drafted in cooler language.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d478:
What Polish democrats wanted is summed up in this cable from Grew of February 6, 1945. The summary covers a memorandum by former Premier Mikolajczyk. The Polish people at home, it said, desired to regulate Polish-Soviet relations. They feared Poland would be forced into communism. Their hopes of independence rested on Britain and the United States.

The memorandum urged a guarantee by all three great powers. Frontier changes should embrace all frontiers at once. The eastern frontier should be settled by compromise, not unilateral dictation, and should favor Poland more than the Curzon Line did. Restitution should include Danzig and East Prussia. Grew's summary reached Yalta as the leaders drew the map the memorandum dreaded.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d78:
Ambassador Harriman appealed to Soviet official Andrei Vyshinsky in a letter dated June 19, 1945. The letter is document 78 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Eisenhower needed his advance party in Berlin the next day. They had to prepare housing, food, and communications for the American delegation. But the Soviet General Staff wanted to wait for Zhukov's return on June 28.

Harriman sets out the request in detail: General Parks, 50 officers, 175 enlisted men, and 50 trucks. He also asks free use of the Dessau-Berlin highway and the Halle-Berlin air route. A little over two weeks after June 28, he argues, would not leave enough time to get ready. He asks for approval that night so the movement can start in the morning.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d178:
General Eisenhower suggested putting the Danube question on the summit agenda in a message dated July 3, 1945. Only a paraphrased extract is printed, as document 178 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears in the second volume, as an enclosure to another document.

The surviving lines discuss an international problem: the internationalization of the Danube river. They say its urgency would suggest adding it to the agenda of the coming Big Three conference, if that action is thought proper. Control of the Danube, Europe's great east-west waterway, was contested ground. The Soviet Union dominated its lower course, while the Western powers wanted the river opened to free navigation. Even this fragment shows a field commander feeding a policy question up to the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d278:
A briefing paper described the pending Austrian occupation zones in a paper dated June 23, 1945. The paper is document 278 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the agreements the European Advisory Commission was finishing in London for Austria's zones of occupation and control machinery.

The zones are largely settled. Salzburg and Upper Austria south of the Danube go to the United States. Burgenland and Lower Austria go to the Soviets. Styria and Carinthia go to the British. The Tirol and Vorarlberg go to the French. The one main obstacle is the zoning of Vienna itself. After a recent reconnaissance mission, most differences look solvable except the airfields. Washington, London, and Paris each press for a field of their own near the capital. Moscow has so far offered only one field for all three. Talks to settle the point were under way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d378:
Notes on reparation, drafted at Babelsberg on July 14, 1945, try to fix the scope of the term before any division among claimants. Agreement, the paper argues, should first be sought on how reparation relates to other forms of compensation by Germany. Only then should the allies argue over shares.

War booty, it says, should be defined narrowly, ideally as only the equipment and supplies of the German armed forces. The net value of labor services by Germans outside Germany should be credited to the reparations account. Restitution should count both property Germany destroyed and property it carried off. The paper was used the next day with the British.

A poem of the soul's climb frames the whole text. John glosses each line to teach how to drop all ties to sense and self. The dark night, he says, strips the soul bare for union with God. The book stands with his Dark Night as a peak of Spain's soul lore.
mackey-encyclopedia-freemasonry-1878:
Albert G. Mackey was the great voice of Masonic lore in the States. His Encyclopedia of Freemasonry came out in 1878. Its full title adds the kindred sciences to the craft. The book aims to hold all a Mason might need to know in one tome.

Heads run from rites and signs to lives of famed Masons of the past. Long tales give the craft's past, its laws, and the sense of its marks. Mackey writes with care and with love for the lore. The book stayed the stock desk guide for the craft for scores of years.
geber-works-russell-1678:
Richard Russell gave The Works of Geber English dress in 1678. Geber was the Latin name for tracts tied to Jabir ibn Hayyan. The core work is the Summa Perfectionis, the Sum of Perfection. It is a root text of the alchemy of the West.

Clear rules tell how to test, purge, and join the base stuffs of the art. Geber gives the first clear tale of strong acids and their use. He sorts metals by their make and tells how each may be raised. The book set the lab craft of alchemy on a firm base.
burckhardt-renaissance-middlemore-1878:
Jacob Burckhardt's The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy appears in S. G. C. Middlemore's translation of 1878. Burckhardt, a Swiss historian, in effect invented the Renaissance as a concept. He portrays Italy from 1300 to 1500 as the birthplace of the modern individual. The state as a work of art opens his account.

Later parts treat discovery of the world and of man, society, festivals, and morals. Burckhardt writes cultural history, not a chain of battles and kings. His method founded a whole field of study. Scholars have revised his picture for a century without displacing it. The book remains cultural history's founding masterpiece in elegant English dress.
barclay-talmud-1878:
Joseph Barclay was the Anglican bishop of Jerusalem when he published The Talmud in 1878. His book gives selections from the Mishnah and the Talmud for Christian readers new to rabbinic literature. Barclay knew Hebrew and lived among the communities whose ancestors wrote the texts.

He translates passages on worship, charity, civil law, and the festivals, with notes explaining customs as he met them in Jerusalem. His aim is fair description rather than the attacks on the Talmud common in older Christian writing. The book stands as an early Christian introduction to the rabbinic tradition by a resident bishop.
bunyan-pilgrims-progress-1678:
John Bunyan was an English tinker and preacher who spent years in jail for preaching without a license. He wrote The Pilgrim's Progress during his imprisonment, and it was published in 1678. The story is told as a dream the narrator has while traveling.

A man named Christian flees the City of Destruction, carrying a heavy burden on his back. On the road to the Celestial City he meets helpers and dangers, from the Slough of Despond to Vanity Fair. Each place stands for a stage of the Christian life. Few books in English have been read by so many people, for so long.
hardy-return-native-1878:
Thomas Hardy published The Return of the Native in 1878, setting it on the wild Egdon Heath in his fictional Wessex. Hardy knew this Dorset landscape from childhood. The heath itself broods over the story almost like a character.

Clym Yeobright, the native, returns from Paris hoping to teach the local people. He marries the restless Eustacia Vye, who dreams only of escaping the heath for a glamorous life. Their mismatch pulls in a former lover, a reddleman, and Clym's stern mother. Misread letters and chance meetings steer everyone toward tragedy. The novel is one of Hardy's most admired studies of longing and fate.
james-daisy-miller-1878:
Henry James published Daisy Miller in 1878, first in an English magazine after American editors balked. James was then an expatriate writer shuttling between America and Europe. The novella made his name on both sides of the Atlantic and defined his great theme: the American abroad.

Daisy Miller, a pretty, free-spirited girl from Schenectady, tours Switzerland and Rome with no sense of European rules. The young American Winterbourne watches her, torn between attraction and the colony's snobbish verdict. Her friendship with an Italian escort ruins her name, and a Roman fever ends the story. James never quite says whether Daisy was innocent or foolish. Readers have argued it for a century.
lessing-dramatic-works-bell-1878:
Ernest Bell's Dramatic Works of Lessing, published in 1878, holds four plays that remade German drama. Miss Sara Sampson brought everyday middle-class sorrow to the stage in place of kings. Philotas gives a captured young prince one fierce choice about honor and death.

Emilia Galotti, the darkest of the four, shows a prince's lust destroying a virtuous girl and her family. Nathan the Wise closes the volume with its plea for tolerance among faiths. Bell's Nathan differs from Taylor's older version, and the two are kept as distinct translations. Together the four plays show why Lessing is counted the founder of modern German drama. No other single volume shows his range so well.
turgenev-dream-tales-1878:
Dream Tales and Prose Poems gathers Turgenev's late, strange writings in Constance Garnett's English. The dream tales let ghosts, visions, and doubles walk through his usual clear prose. A realist by trade, Turgenev here explores the fears and wonders that reason leaves unexplained.

The prose poems, written near the end of his life, are brief meditations in lyrical form. They treat age, death, Russia, language, and the small mercies of daily life. One famous piece praises the Russian language itself as a stay in dark times. The volume shows the visionary underside of a writer famed for balance. It closes Garnett's Turgenev with his most personal pages.
haug-essays-sacred-language-parsis-1878:
Martin Haug's Essays on the Sacred Language, Writings, and Religion of the Parsis appeared at London in 1878. The second edition was edited and enlarged by E. W. West. Haug, a German scholar who worked in India, founded the Western study of the Avesta, the Zoroastrian scriptures. His essays sort the Gathas, the oldest hymns ascribed to Zoroaster himself, from later layers of the texts.

An outline of a Pahlavi-Pazand glossary closes the volume, a tool for students of Middle Persian. Haug's work established Pahlavi studies and put Parsi religion on a scholarly footing in Europe. The book became the most cited nineteenth-century work on its subject. West's enlargement kept it current after Haug's early death. It still introduces the field's history.
davila-civil-wars-of-france-1678:
Enrico Caterino Davila, an Italian soldier who served at the side of Henri IV, wrote his Historia delle guerre civili di Francia in 1630. The English translation by Charles Cotterell and William Aylesbury, first made in 1647, appears here in the 1678 printing. Davila had seen the French wars of religion as a young man in the king's service.

His history covers the long struggle between crown, Catholics, and Huguenots that tore France apart. He writes as both witness and analyst, weighing causes with a soldier's knowledge of camps and courts. The book became the classic near-contemporary history of those wars. Its balance and detail kept it in readers' hands for two centuries.
champlain-voyages-slafter-vol-1-1878:
Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec and spent his life mapping and settling New France. His Voyages, first issued from 1613 onward, tell that work in his own words. Volume one here follows the Prince Society translation of 1878 to 1882, with Charles P Otis translating and Edmund F Slafter editing.

Champlain writes as explorer, sailor, and governor at once: coasts sounded, rivers traced, alliances made with native nations. His account is the primary record of early Canada and the Great Lakes country. No later history of French Canada can start anywhere else. The first volume opens the fullest English edition of the founder's own story, plain and exact.
champlain-voyages-slafter-vol-2-1878:
Volume two of the Prince Society Champlain continues the Voyages of Samuel de Champlain, the founder of New France. The translation of 1878 to 1882, by Charles P Otis under Edmund F Slafter's editorship, spans Champlain's works of 1613 to 1632. Volume two stands at the middle of the three-volume English set.

Champlain's narrative mixes sea craft, diplomacy, and the hard logistics of planting a colony in a cold land. He records his dealings with the native nations of Canada and the Great Lakes in detail. His maps and reports guided French policy for a generation. This volume keeps the primary record of early Canada moving, in the founder's own measured voice.
champlain-voyages-slafter-vol-3-1878:
The Prince Society translation of Champlain's Voyages closes with volume three. Samuel de Champlain's works run from 1613 to 1632. Charles P Otis Englished them, and Edmund F Slafter edited the set between 1878 and 1882. Together they tell the founding of New France from the founder's own desk, in three volumes.

Champlain governed Quebec through hunger, war, and fragile peace with native nations and English rivals. His last writings show a colony still small but rooted, and a founder still planning its growth. The Voyages remain the primary record of early Canada and the Great Lakes. Volume three completes the standard English set, ending where Champlain's own work ends.
whitehurst-inquiry-original-state-earth-:
John Whitehurst, a Derbyshire clockmaker and naturalist, inquired into the Earth's first state in 1778. His Inquiry treats strata, underground fire, and the Deluge in one scheme. Whitehurst had mapped the layered rocks of Derbyshire with a surveyor's care. Those strata, he argues, record the Earth's formation in stages.

Subterranean heat raises and breaks the crust in his account. The Deluge still plays its part, though nature's agents grow larger beside it. The book bridges the old diluvial theories and the coming geological revolution. Hutton and his age stood not far ahead. Whitehurst's plates of strata served later geologists well. His county pride and exact eye fill the work.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1878 the eighth volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica came off the press. The set was nearing its end, yet the method never thins: full proving records, sorted by remedy and region. Allen's wide net caught symptoms from famous provers and obscure ones alike, all filed in order.

Working doctors used the volumes when a case turned on some small, strange sign. The odds were good that Allen had filed that sign somewhere in the ten volumes. Volume VIII, like its mates, asks patience and pays it back in depth, a reference shelf that later short guides could never replace.

Volume IX of Allen's Encyclopaedia, dated 1878, stands one step from the end of the ten-volume record. Its remedy entries hold the same wealth: every prover's symptom, placed by body region, with its source named. The alphabetical march of drugs across the whole set continues through these pages.

Allen's restraint as an editor is the set's quiet strength throughout. He lets contradictions stand, since real provers differ, and leaves judgment to the prescriber at the desk. Students of the school's history read these volumes to see drug pictures whole, before later authors boiled them down to keynotes.
plos-pone-0003378:
Raúl Alelú-Paz and co-authors improved a staining method for brain tissue in this 2008 paper. Staining lets scientists see one chosen protein inside a slice of tissue. Fixing chemicals used to store human brains tend to hide those proteins. For thirty years, that masking effect had limited work on stored brain samples.

The team presents a new way to unmask the hidden proteins before staining. Their method brought back clear signals in human brain tissue. Stored brains are a key resource for studying diseases of the mind and nerves. A better unmasking step means old samples can answer new questions.
plos-pone-0003478:
Vijay Chickarmane and Carsten Peterson modeled early cell fate choices in this 2008 paper. Three factors, Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog, form a self-reinforcing network in stem cells. That network keeps embryonic stem cells able to renew and stay flexible. Rival signals between factors push cells toward fixed roles.

Their computational model follows that tug of war in time. It shows how cells settle as stem cells, trophectoderm, or endoderm. Trophectoderm and endoderm are two early embryo layers. The model captures the logic behind life's first branching choices. The same three factors are still core tools in stem cell labs today.
plos-pone-0003578:
Josef Wagner and co-authors searched gut biopsies from children with Crohn's disease in this 2008 paper. Reading bacterial 16S ribosomal genes can identify gut flora members. That method had already implicated some bacterial families in bowel inflammation. The team used ileal biopsies, from the last part of the small gut.

They identified and characterized Pseudomonas DNA in those samples. Finding this germ adds to the microbial census of Crohn's. Gut flora composition may shape inflammatory bowel disease in the young. Each named suspect narrows the hunt for triggers. Crohn's often starts in youth and lasts for life, with flares and calm spells.
plos-pone-0003678:
Alex Proekt, Jane Wong, Yuriy Zhurov, and colleagues published this theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008. An animal's nervous system does not act alone; it stays coupled to its surroundings at every moment. That coupling limits the dynamics both sides must have for adaptive behavior to arise.

Building on earlier computer work, the authors derive which dynamical properties the nervous system needs. From those properties, they show, suitable behavior in the environment can be predicted. The study reads smart behavior out of the shared physics of brain and world, rather than from the brain alone.
plos-pone-0003778:
Hugh R. Woodland and Andrew M. Fry published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Centrioles are small barrels that organize cells and build cilia and flagella. Pix proteins are parts of vertebrate centrioles found in most eukaryotes. The authors made a wide survey across the tree of life.

They mapped where Pix proteins occur and how their forms vary between organisms. Alongside, they surveyed which organisms carry flagella, cilia, and centrioles, using published records. The census clarifies how these ancient structures arose and diversified across eukaryotes. The Pix family now has a map for deeper study.
plos-pone-0003878:
Christopher E. Bagwell, Swapna Bhat, Gary M. Hawkins, and co-authors sequenced a tough bacterium in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article reports the genome of Kineococcus radiotolerans SRS30216. The microbe came from a high-level radioactive waste site at Savannah River. It withstands gamma radiation at levels close to the famous Deinococcus radiodurans.

The U.S. Department of Energy Joint Genome Institute carried out the sequencing. Reading the full genome lets scientists hunt for genes behind the extreme resistance. Those genes could guide cleanup methods for nuclear waste sites. They may also suggest new uses in industry where radiation harms other microbes.
plos-pone-0003978:
Adrian Nestor, Jean M. Vettel, and Michael J. Tarr studied how face tasks shape brain coding in 2008. Faces are sorted in many ways, which strains recognition systems. Two basic tasks are spotting a face and telling which face it is. The authors asked whether those tasks need different codes.

Their PLOS ONE article explores how task demands reshape feature use. Detection may lean on broad cues, while individuation needs fine detail. Neural patterns shifted with the task a person was doing. The work shows face reading is flexible, not one fixed process. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004078:
Hui Wang and Dimitrios Vavylonis modeled actin cable building in fission yeast in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The formin protein For3p starts actin cables at yeast cell tips. Those cables guide growth toward the cell ends. Prior experiments hinted at how assembly might proceed.

Their model tests whether For3p behavior can explain cable growth. It joins For3p placement, actin polymerization, and cable movement in one scheme. A working model predicts what new experiments should measure. It shows how simple protein rules yield ordered cell structures. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004178:
Yungok Ihm and colleagues published this structural study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rev is a regulatory protein that equine infectious anemia virus, a relative of HIV, cannot do without. It grabs viral RNA messages that are not fully spliced. It then escorts them out of the nucleus. That step is required before the virus can build its structural proteins.

No full picture of this protein's shape existed. The team built a structural model of Rev from the horse virus. A model of how Rev is folded helps scientists compare it with the HIV version and understand how this viral switch works.
plos-pone-0004278:
Olivier Béaslas and colleagues published this gut study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The intestine absorbs dietary lipids and delivers them to the body as triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. How enterocytes, the intestine's absorptive cells, regulate that process matters, because long post-meal spikes in blood lipids are harmful.

The team describe a new role for SR-BI, also called CLA-1, a receptor best known from cholesterol handling. They present it as a sensor of dietary lipids in enterocytes. A gut sensor that tastes incoming fat could be a target for controlling blood lipids after meals.
plos-pone-0004378:
Public health teams watch for disease outbreaks as early as they can. One newer signal is what sick people type into medical web sites. Anette Hulth, Gustaf Rydevik, and Annika Linde tested that signal in Sweden. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used flu as the test case. They studied queries sent to a medical web site.

The authors asked whether flu-related searches rise and fall with real flu spread. Search data arrives fast and costs little to collect. If queries track illness well, they can support older reporting systems. The paper is an early test of web data for outbreak watching. It helped pave the way for later digital disease tracking work.
plos-pone-0004478: In 2009, Essafi-Benkhadir, Grosso, and Puissant found a gene with two faces. The Sp3 transcription factor both induced apoptosis and marked tumour aggressiveness. The double agent killed cells yet flagged danger. The finding clarifies Sp3's debated role. The marker may guide prognosis.
plos-pone-0004578: In 2009, Wu, Jin, and Xiong built a neat math tool for tricky gene and place puzzles. Mutual information tested gene and place interaction rigorously. The clever measure defined and detected interactions cleanly. The method aids complex-trait genetics research today. The exact definition matters most greatly.
plos-pone-0004678: In 2009, Gregory, Willis, and Jiguet built a climate gauge from European bird counts. An indicator of climate change impact on European bird populations was created. The bird trends tracked warming closely. The tool informs conservation policy. The change is rapid.
plos-pone-0004778: In 2009, a team linked immune gene variants to TB harm anew here. Immune gene spellings across TB stages in Pakistani patients were mapped. The variants tracked harm quite closely. The study guides TB care research. The TB burden is high indeed.
zola-love-episode-1878:
Starkweather's English version of A Love Episode came from a 1905 fine edition with Dantan's pictures. Only five hundred numbered copies were registered for that printing. Twenty-six chapters carry Zola's most delicate novel of 1878.

Helene Grandjean, a widowed mother in Passy, has buried her heart with her husband. Her daughter's illness brings the kind Dr. Deberle into the house. Love ambushes them both before either can guard against it. The slow tale tracks a woman's awakening against the shifting seasons of Paris. No other volume in the saga is so quiet, so tender, or so purely romantic in feeling.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol1-1878:
Travers Twiss edited Bracton's De legibus et consuetudinibus Angliae for the Rolls Series, and the first volume appeared in 1878. Henry de Bracton, a thirteenth-century judge, wrote the treatise as a full account of English law. It is the first great book of the common law, and Twiss gave it a scholarly text with the Latin and English side by side.

Volume 1 lays out the treatise's opening: the kinds of law, the courts, and the first principles of property and persons. Bracton insists that the king himself stands under God and the law, a line quoted for centuries afterward. The treatise draws on real cases from the plea rolls, not just theory. Twiss's edition made the foundation book of English law usable by modern scholars.
price-free-discussion-materialism-1778:
Price and Joseph Priestley argued the nature of the soul in print. Their exchange appeared in 1778 as A Free Discussion of the Doctrines of Materialism and Philosophical Necessity. Both men were dissenting ministers and friends, which made the fight livelier: the dissenter against the dissenter, mind against matter. Priestley held that mind is a power of organized matter; Price defended an immaterial soul.

The letters also take up necessity, the claim that every act is fixed by prior causes, which Price feared would dissolve moral responsibility. The two friends argue hard and stay friends, a model of public controversy. The book preserves the liveliest theological debate of its age in open letters. It shows Enlightenment religion arguing with itself, in public, at full strength.
cia-0000009778:
Laos is the setting for a March 1973 sighting of two American prisoners of war. The heading gives no province, which makes this one of the file's less placed reports. It arrived weeks after the Paris accords and the start of prisoner homecoming.

Unplaced sightings were the hardest to use, yet they were never thrown away. A detail inside the report might later match a camp or a route. Laotian cases stayed open longer than Vietnamese ones as a rule. This file keeps a thin report alive for that later matching, part of Laos's long unfinished accounting.
cia-0000009878:
American prisoners were reportedly detained by the Viet Cong in Tay Ninh province, an August 1966 report states. Tay Ninh, northwest of Saigon near the Cambodian border, held the Viet Cong's southern headquarters region. Prisoners taken near Saigon often vanished into that border system.

Reported detention is weaker than a sighting, and the heading keeps the hedge. Even so, Tay Ninh claims matched the known geography of southern captivity. Officials filed them for comparison with border camp reports. This early southern file shows the prison map forming in 1966, hedges and all, around the capital's own province.
cia-0000010478:
Iran's position in the East-West conflict is set out in a March 1951 CIA paper. Iran bordered the Soviet Union along a long northern frontier and held vast oil fields in the south. That geography made the country a prize neither bloc could ignore.

The paper weighs the shah's government, the nationalist movement, and Soviet pressure as parts of one problem. Weeks later, oil nationalization would seize the world's headlines. Analysts writing in March already framed Iran as a front line. This file preserves that framing at the Cold War's Persian front, before the crisis broke open.
cia-0000012278:
Vladimir I. Toumanoff sat for a debriefing in September 1960, and the CIA record of it survives with its subject partly blanked. Toumanoff was a Russian-born American who had crossed paths with figures in the Penkovsky affair. Debriefers asked him about a matter the released file will not name, blacked out in the title itself.

The record preserves the questions asked and the answers a witness gave while events were fresh. Such accounts formed the human foundation under the case's grander papers. For readers, it shows how the biggest spy case of the era was built partly from small testimonies like this one.
cia-0000012378:
Penkovskiy Case: the whole operation gets its plain title in a CIA overview from June 1963. By then the story had run its arc, from the colonel's first approach to his arrest and trial in Moscow. An overview written that summer could survey the case whole, as its handlers first understood it complete, with the ending known and the costs counted.

Such surveys became the service's own account of its greatest success and sharpest loss. They fixed the narrative officers would teach from for years. For readers, this is the closest thing to a definitive telling by the men who ran him.
cia-0000014778: Communists at a Rockefeller Colloquium are named in a CIA file dated July 3, 1953. The file calls Bernal and Wooster Communist sympathizers at the meeting. Scholars and scientists at such gatherings drew files when their politics seemed left. The record shows how deep the watch reached into lecture halls and labs.
cia-0000015378: A reported sighting of unconventional aircraft fills a CIA file dated September 3, 1955. Reported is the careful word; no one swore to the craft. The fall of 1955 brought a fresh crop of such claims. This file holds one of them, worded with the era's full and careful caution. The September sighting report is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015478: Sightings from January 19 to May 15, 1954, are gathered in a CIA record of unidentified flying objects. The title's own span is used here, since an older summary gave a shorter one. Four months of reports in one bundle let readers judge pace and pattern. Spring brought a fresh crop of claims, and the agency counted them like the seasons before.
cia-0000016878: How well Vietnamese communist forces could keep fighting in South Vietnam is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1967. Such papers measured troops, supply, losses, and will to fight. In 1967 the war was growing, and sound judgment of enemy strength carried grave weight. The clipped title marks the paper as an original study, a core task of the agency's analysts.
cia-0000042878:
El Salvador: Update on the Jesuit Killings, number 6, is a CIA record dated April 4, 1990. By the sixth update, the case was months old and still open. The series had become the case's public diary in brief form.

Inside, the latest position of the investigation is recorded. Spring updates dealt with courts, custody, and slow legal motion. The file shows the case settling into its long middle passage. Headlines had faded by the spring, yet the numbered briefs kept coming on schedule. Their steady rhythm is itself evidence of how long justice took in this case.
cia-0000044478:
R. Zamora was interviewed on the killing of the Jesuit priests, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. The file is a second interview record under nearly the same title. Zamora spoke for the political opposition in El Salvador.

Inside, his account of the case is given again, weeks into the new year. Repetition let the opposition keep its charge before the public. Each interview sharpened the case against the army's account. The file shows that pressure being maintained on purpose, so the murders could not sink from view while the courts moved at their own slow pace.
cia-0000045978: Diplomats commented on a photograph said to show living American servicemen still held after the Vietnam War. A CIA item dated June 6, 1991, kept their reactions. A claim of living prisoners was the most charged kind in the missing-men dispute. The comments show officials abroad weighing the picture's power against the thin proof behind it.
cia-0000049078: El Salvador's chief of staff gave his views on criticism of the military high command in a CIA item from 1984. The criticism, much of it from Washington, blamed the command for abuses it refused to punish. His answer, preserved here, shows the brass defending its honor while the war's record grew darker.
cia-0000049178: The Joint General Staff headquarters in El Salvador evaluated public comments by a former colonel in a CIA item from 1990. A retired officer speaking out could wound the institution more than any enemy broadcast. The evaluation shows the brass grading one of their own, in the war's last, touchy phase.
cia-0000049278: A House intelligence staffer named Giza sent a follow-up request in 1985 about the Honduran death squad investigation, and a CIA item preserves it. Follow-ups were oversight's teeth: the second letter, asking why the first went unanswered. The item shows a staffer keeping a hard case alive across the years.
cia-0000049378: Guerrillas planning assassinations in El Salvador is the warning carried by declassified CIA document 0000049378, dated November 4, 1988. The item is marked for the Truth Commission and centers on a reported guerrilla plan. It survives as a brief dated notice, its title stating the alleged plot plainly for anyone tracing the agency's late-war Salvadoran reporting.
cia-0000075278: Pro-Cominform Communist Party protest of the Rosenberg sentences is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075278, dated October 1, 1952. The heading names the protesting party line and the sentences being protested. Readers find a short declassified item from the early Cold War, preserved as a record of organized protest rather than a report on the case itself.

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1278:
President Truman wrote to Generalissimo Stalin on 21 July 1945. Leader-to-leader notes were the summit's most direct channel. This one went from the American president to the Soviet chief in the middle of the talks' first week.

Such a message carried the sender's personal weight. It could soften a session, press a claim, or test the other man's mood between meetings. This note belongs to the pair of Truman-Stalin exchanges in the volume. Read with Stalin's reply of the following week, it shows the top of the alliance at work in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1378:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference's central secretariat, wrote a memorandum on 9 August 1945, a week after Potsdam ended. The secretariat kept the summit's records, lists, and drafts in order. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Papers written after a conference closes often explain how its texts were made and filed. Yost's post at the secretariat put him at the center of that housekeeping. His memorandum helps readers trust the record itself, since it comes from the man charged with keeping it. It is a fitting late entry in the volume: the staff view of how a great meeting was wound up and its papers put away.
frus-1945-50-intel-d78:
McCormack wrote to William Benton, assistant secretary for public and cultural relations, on 23 October 1945. Both men ran newish empires inside the State Department, Benton's being information and culture. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Where intelligence ends and public information begins was a live border question in 1945, since wartime agencies had mixed spying, analysis, and propaganda. McCormack writing to Benton shows the two office heads sorting that border between them. Readers get a look at a forgotten seam of the postwar build. The men who told America's story abroad had to share a department with the men who read the world's secrets. Neither side could swallow the other.
frus-1945-50-intel-d178:

In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 178, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d278:

Readers meet it as document 278 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1861-d78:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 September 1861. The dispatch is document 78 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Adams letters in three days mark a full week at the London post. Notes, calls, and press talk filled the envoy's days. The second letter shows how fast fresh points could pile up, each one needing a clear report home. Fast work in September kept the small points from growing into open quarrels. Small points, met fast, stayed small; that was the whole art of the autumn.
frus-1861-d178:
A letter of 3 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 178 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September orders to Spain dealt with the watch on ports and trade. Cuba's harbors lay close to the blockade's edge. Seward's letter kept Schurz alert to any Spanish step that might let Southern ships find shelter or supplies. Cuba's governor took orders from Madrid, which made Schurz's post a guard on the island too. A guard on the island, kept by letter, cost the Union no ships at all.
frus-1861-d278:

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d78:

The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d178:

The end of October found the French plan for a joint truce proposal nearly ready, while Britain hung back. Adams's reports from these days are prized because he heard British doubts at close range. This letter forms part of the closing record of October, the month when European action on the war came closest and then began to recede. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d278:

Seward's letters of this period, this one among them, probed that opening while keeping formal ties smooth with the French government. frus-1862-d478:
On 11 August 1862 James E. Harvey reported from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 478 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Harvey wrote in the weeks when the Confederate cruiser Alabama had just slipped to sea and begun her raids. Portuguese waters, including the Azores, were among the places such ships might use. A report from Lisbon in that month spoke directly to the Union's effort against the raiders. The Union hoped to hem them in by law. It could not reach them by force. Harvey's letters give the State Department's side of that effort, from one of the ports where it was actually decided.
frus-1862-d578:
On 23 July 1862 James Watson Webb reported from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 578 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Webb's July reports came as the war at sea was spreading south in prospect. Confederate cruisers were fitting out to raid American commerce. Their hunting ground would be the ocean routes. Brazil's many ports could shelter such ships or shut them out, depending on the rules Rio enforced. A minister's report on Brazilian intentions was therefore practical intelligence, not ceremony. The letter belongs to the maritime side of the volume, where the Union fought to turn neutral law into a wall around its merchant fleet.
frus-1862-d678:
Anson Burlingame wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 July 1862. The dispatch comes from Burlingame's post as American minister to China. It is document 678 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, in the heart of the summer mail.

Summer letters from China brought word on trade and on the Qing court's long fight with the Taiping revolt. Burlingame's reports also served Americans who lived and traded in the treaty ports, whose safety rested on his work. This dispatch is one of the last in his 1862 run, and it shows an envoy settled into the rhythm of a hard, distant post.
frus-1863p1-d78:

A three-letter day at the legation meant a full plate: talks, papers, and people to report on. Adams kept each sheet to its own head, a habit that makes his file easy to read still. frus-1863p1-d178:

frus-1863p1-d278: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 September 1863. frus-1863p1-d478:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 25 April 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d578:
Secretary William H. Seward addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 25 June 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d678:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 30 November 1863. The letter appears as document 678 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. Adams was the main American voice in Britain through the whole Civil War.

The Union's great fear was that Britain might back the South or treat it as a full nation. Seward's London mail worked against that risk day after day. This dispatch is one small part of that steady push. Read with its neighbors, it helps show how talks stayed open and calm even while a hard war went on at home.
plos-pbio-0020078:
Habibeh Khoshbouei, Namita Sen, Bipasha Guptaroy, and others studied the dopamine transporter in PLOS Biology in 2004. This protein normally clears dopamine, a key brain signal, from the gap between nerve cells. Amphetamine flips its action and pushes dopamine out instead.

The team found that a phosphate tag on the transporter's front end is needed for that flip. Without the tag, amphetamine cannot trigger the outflow. The detail matters for understanding how stimulant drugs work at the molecular level. It also marks a possible control point. A drug that guards that tag might blunt amphetamine's effects while leaving normal dopamine clearing intact.
plos-pbio-0020178:

The switch is a protein called Hairy, which turns target genes off during embryo growth. The authors found which genes Hairy binds and which helper proteins it recruits.

A switch is only as good as the helpers it brings to each site. By listing targets and helpers together, the study shows how one protein can fine-tune many genes in different ways. That matters because Hairy-like switches shape body plans in many animals. The fly data gives a concrete parts list for a whole class of gene control.
plos-pone-0000078:
Marco Marani, Tommaso Zillio, Enrica Belluco, and their team modeled plant growth patterns in PLOS ONE in 2006. In marshes and other wetlands, plants form stripes and patches that long puzzled observers. Older models treated the pattern as a neutral result of random spread. The authors show that view falls short.

Their work argues the patterns are non-neutral: feedback between plants and water flow shapes them. Plants slow the water, trap soil, and change their own living conditions, which then drives the stripes. Getting the cause right matters for restoring wetlands, since planting by the wrong model wastes effort. The paper is a case for active feedback in ecology.
plos-pone-0000178:
Hany A. El-Shemy, Ahmed M. Aboul-Enein, Khalid Mostafa Aboul-Enein, and colleagues published this pharmacology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports that extracts from willow leaves contain agents that act against tumors. The extracts were tested against three cell types and showed anti-tumor effects.

Willow already gave medicine aspirin, so its leaves are a plausible place to look for active compounds. The authors screen the extracts and report the killing effect on the tested cells. Work at this stage is an early filter: it cannot prove a drug, but it flags plant chemistry worth isolating and testing further.
plos-pone-0000278:
Colleen V. Chien published this health policy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It compares brand-name and generic supply of HIV/AIDS drugs for sub-Saharan Africa, where the epidemic hit hardest and drug access was a global controversy. The author asks how the two supply routes stack up in getting medicines to patients.

Price was only part of the access problem; supply chains, patents, and donations all played roles. The paper compares the brand and generic channels directly. It contributed evidence to the debate over how poor countries should source life-saving drugs, a question that shaped global health policy.
plos-pone-0000378:
Kun-Lin Zhang and colleagues built a model of a human defense protein, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, APOBEC3G, is part of the body's built-in defense against viruses such as HIV, which fights back with a protein of its own. Knowing the defender's three-dimensional shape is key to understanding that struggle.

Since a full experimental structure was not in hand, the team modeled the protein's structure from related knowledge. A model like this gives researchers a working picture. It shows which parts of the protein do the antiviral work. It also shows where a virus might attack it. Such models often guide lab experiments and, later, drug design.
plos-pone-0000478:
Marcin R. Przewloka and colleagues took apart the kinetochore of the fruit fly piece by piece, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The kinetochore is the protein machine that grips chromosomes and hauls them apart during cell division. Their molecular analysis covered the composition and assembly of its core in Drosophila melanogaster.

Knowing which proteins form the core, and in what order they assemble, is basic to understanding how division stays accurate. Errors here leave cells with missing or extra chromosomes. Fly kinetochores offer a simpler model of the same machine that operates in human cells, where its failure is tied to cancer and birth defects.
plos-pone-0000578:
